subtitulo: How a sixty-year fracture is deliberately closed, and why Peru did not do the same (1974–1981)

coda.heading: Coda for the trip: what to look for

items.text: In Athens, the Parliament building in Syntagma — the former royal palace of Otto, turned into a legislative seat: the imported monarchy of dispatch 16 now housing the republic that abolished it — and the square itself, the setting for every mobilization from 1843 to 2011 and 2025. It is the place where Greek politics becomes visible; if you happen upon any gathering, watch it closely: Greek demonstration culture is dense, ritualized and very different from the Peruvian kind.

And a useful question to raise in conversation: what the year 1974 means to whoever you're talking with. You'll find it comes up as a sharp dividing line — "before the Metapolitefsi," "after" — the same way Peru speaks of "before" and "after" other dates. How a society periodizes its own time is one of the best ethnographic entry points there is, and it requires asking nothing delicate.

closing: Notice too the party initials painted on the walls: you'll see PASOK and KKE with a persistence that's surprising, in a city where political graffiti is an active medium of communication and not a leftover. The KKE, legalized in 1974 after twenty-seven years of proscription, still exists, with offices, a newspaper and unions: the continuity of an organization defeated in a civil war eighty years ago is a striking fact about how conflicts get closed without erasing the actors.

sections.heading: Six decisions in seven years
paragraphs: The Greek transition is usually told as the return of a statesman. It is more useful to read it as a sequence of concrete political decisions, taken in order, each with a cost, which together dismantled the regime described in the three preceding dispatches.

First: in September 1974, Karamanlis LEGALIZED THE COMMUNIST PARTY, banned since 1947. It was done by a conservative politician, a leader of the right who had governed in the fifties within the victors' system, and against the judgment of much of his own camp. The argument was simple: a regime that excludes a third of its society is not stable.

Second: on December 8, 1974, a referendum was held on the form of the state. The monarchy — which had taken part in the 1916 Schism, in the fraudulent restoration of 1935, in the Metaxas dictatorship of 1936, in the crisis of 1965 and, with the king in exile, in the coup of 1967 — was abolished by around sixty-nine percent of the vote. The result was accepted without challenge, and with it the monarchist-republican divide that had structured Greek politics for sixty years was closed.
Third: in 1975 a republican constitution was promulgated, still in force with amendments.

Fourth: in August 1975 the leaders of the 1967 coup and those responsible for the repression of the Polytechnic and for the torture were put on trial. There were death sentences commuted to life imprisonment; the principal leaders died in prison. The purge of the armed forces and the police, by contrast, was limited: the official formula was that the guilty were few, and with it institutional continuity was protected.
Fifth: in 1982, with PASOK now in government, the National Resistance was legally recognized, placing ELAS combatants on an equal footing with the rest, thirty-eight years on.
Sixth: in 1989, a coalition government of right and left — unthinkable a decade earlier — agreed to destroy the police files of political convictions.

None of these decisions was obvious or costless. All of them were taken against sectors of the very coalition that adopted them. And together they constitute what the literature on transitions calls a CLOSURE PACT: not an emotional reconciliation, but the withdrawal from the legal order of the categories that made part of the population an internal enemy.

sections.heading: What the pact did not do
paragraphs: It is worth not idealizing it, because the price was high and it was paid later.

The limited purge left in the state officials, police and judges trained under the previous regime. Justice for torture reached some of the direct perpetrators and not the apparatus. The civil war was not publicly processed for decades: it remained a family matter, silent, and its critical historiography only developed from the eighties and nineties onward. And the recognition of the Resistance in 1982 came so late that many of its protagonists had already died.

Moreover, the new system rapidly reproduced the structural vice it had carried since 1844: the distribution of public employment as political currency. Andreas Papandreou's PASOK, founded in 1974 and victorious in 1981 on the slogan of Change, integrated the historically excluded sectors — the defeated left, the descendants of the persecuted, the peasantry, second-tier civil servants — largely through access to the state: mass hiring, regularizations, pensions. It was simultaneously a real operation of social justice and the consolidation of a clientelist machine that the right would replicate at every alternation. The fiscal foundations of the 2010 crisis were laid there, and saying so does not amount to endorsing the austerity narrative: the inclusion of the excluded happened through the only channel the country had available.
This is the kind of nuance worth holding on to: the same process can be reparative and dysfunctional at once, and assessments that see only one of the two faces are propaganda.

sections.heading: Europe as insurance against the past
paragraphs: The most important foreign-policy decision of the period was not military. In 1979 Greece signed the treaty of accession to the European Economic Community, with effective entry on January 1, 1981. Karamanlis pushed it through against the opinion of much of the left — PASOK campaigned against it and promised a referendum it never called — and against the technical objections of the Commission itself, which considered the Greek economy insufficiently prepared.

The decisive argument was not economic but political: to ANCHOR Greek democracy within a supranational structure that would make the return of a dictatorship institutionally very costly. Spain and Portugal would make exactly the same calculation in 1986. European integration was, for all three southern countries, insurance against their own recent past.

The price of that insurance was collected thirty years later. The same structure that guaranteed democratic irreversibility imposed, between 2010 and 2018, economic conditions no Greek electorate had voted for and which a referendum went so far as to reject. European membership is simultaneously the guarantee that the colonels will not return and the mechanism by which the fundamental distributive decisions are taken outside the country. There is no logical contradiction between the two: there is an explicit trade-off between sovereignty and stability that Greece accepted in 1979, aware, at least in part, of its terms.

Peru never had that option. There is no integration structure in Latin America with comparable sanctioning power — the Andean Community, Mercosur and the OAS do not come remotely close — and that is why Peru's successive institutional breakdowns, from 1992 through the last decade, found no effective external anchor beyond statements and market reactions. Here the comparison is painful and precise: part of Greek democratic stability is explained not by internal virtues but by an external architecture that imposes costs. The absence of that architecture is one of the structural conditions of Peruvian fragility, and it is not resolved by exhorting the political class.

sections.heading: 1974 and 1980: two transitions, a brutal contrast
paragraphs: Greece regained democracy in July 1974. Peru did so in July 1980, with the handover of power by the military to Fernando Belaúnde after twelve years of military rule.

On May 17, 1980, on the eve of those elections, a group from Sendero Luminoso burned the ballot boxes in Chuschi, province of Cangallo, Ayacucho. It was the first act of the war. In other words: PERU'S DEMOCRATIC TRANSITION AND THE START OF THE INTERNAL ARMED CONFLICT OCCURRED THE SAME WEEK.

The comparison admits no comfort. Greece transitioned from a dictatorship into a democracy that could devote its energies to consolidating, integrating and distributing; Peru transitioned into a democracy that from its very first day had to sustain a war on its poorest territory, and sustained it with a violence that ended up producing most of the victims. Greece closed its civil war thirty years after it ended, through legislative decisions; Peru began its own on the day of its transition. Everything that separates the two countries over the following forty years — the quality of their institutions, the nature of their crises, the availability of the internal enemy as a political category — has one of its roots there.

And there is one further element worth noting: Greece carried out its closure pact in a context of economic growth and the expectation of European integration, that is, with resources to distribute. Closure pacts are easier when there is something to hand out. Peru attempted its own — the CVR in 2003, reparations, reforms — in contexts of scarcity, political fragmentation and no external anchor. This absolves no one of responsibility, but it explains why exhorting reconciliation without material conditions or institutional architecture produces little.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: the exhaustion of the Metapolitefsi
paragraphs: In 2024 the Metapolitefsi turned fifty, and the anniversary reactivated a debate that had been simmering already: whether the political order born in 1974 is still in force, or whether it ended with the 2010 crisis.

The arguments for exhaustion are solid. The PASOK–New Democracy two-party system that structured politics for thirty-five years broke down: PASOK went from governing with more than forty percent of the vote to single digits within a few years. Electoral turnout fell steadily. Trust in parties and in parliament ranks among the lowest in the European Union in Eurobarometer surveys. And the agenda that had defined the pact — democracy, Europe, inclusion through public employment — stopped functioning once Europe itself imposed the dismantling of the third element.

The arguments for continuity are solid too: there was alternation, governments serve out their terms, the far right was prosecuted in the courts — the trial of Golden Dawn, concluded in 2020, declared the party a criminal organization and convicted its leadership, one of the few cases of its kind in Europe — and membership in the Union was never questioned even at the sharpest point of the crisis. The system withstood a test few democracies would have withstood.

Both things are true, and that duality is the subject of the six remaining dispatches. What we will examine starting with the next one is how a country that had carefully built its stability arrived, thirty years later, at the brink of leaving the euro; what was decided, who decided it, and what remained afterward. And we will do so with the Peruvian mirror in place, because Peru went through its own decade of adjustment in the nineties, with comparable instruments and very different political results.
